title: Impact of Earthquake-Related Mass Casualty Burden on Hospital Microbial Ecology and Surgical Site Infections After Elective Orthopaedic Surgery: A Retrospective Cohort Study
abstract: The aim of this study was to compare surgical site infections (SSIs) developing after primary elective orthopaedic procedures before and after the February 6, 2023 earthquakes and to investigate the incidence, causative pathogen distribution, and antimicrobial resistance patterns. This single-center retrospective cohort study included patients undergoing primary total or partial hip arthroplasty, total knee arthroplasty, or open reduction and internal fixation. The Patients were divided into pre-earthquake (June 1, 2018-February 5, 2023) and post-earthquake (June 1, 2023-November 1, 2025) periods. The SSI cases were defined according to periprosthetic joint infection (ICM 2025) and fracture-related infection (FRI 2018) criteria. Microbiological profiles, resistance patterns, and clinical outcomes were compared between groups. A total of 99 and 118 SSI cases were identified in the pre- and post-earthquake cohorts, respectively. Overall SSI rates were similar between groups (0.98% vs. 1.19%; p=0.143). However, post-earthquake infections were associated with significantly longer hospital stays (28 vs. 22 days; p=0.025) and increased debridement procedures (2.0 vs. 1.0; p=0.006). Polymicrobial infections increased significantly (12.1% vs. 23.7%; p=0.028). A marked microbiological shift was observed, with Gram-negative organisms becoming predominant (67.7% vs. 47.6%; p=0.004), while Gram-positive organisms decreased. Staphylococcus aureus isolation significantly declined (35.4% vs. 17.2%; p=0.008). Meticillin resistance among Gram-positive isolates increased (34.9% vs. 60.0%; p=0.022), whereas no significant change in Gram-negative carbapenem resistance was observed. Our study results showed that the rates of polymicrobial infections and meticillin resistance among Gram-positive isolates increased significantly. This microbiological shift was also associated with clinically relevant outcomes, including prolonged hospital stay and an increased number of debridement procedures. Taken together, in centers exposed to a high burden of mass casualty patients, the infection dynamics of routine elective surgical cases may continue to evolve even months after the disaster. Reassessment of existing empirical treatment protocols is warranted in such settings.

title: Unexplained Colistin Resistance in Klebsiella pneumoniae: Insights into sRNA-Mediated Post-Transcriptional Regulation
abstract: Colistin is a last-resort antibiotic used to treat infections caused by multidrug-resistant Gram-negative pathogens, including Klebsiella pneumoniae. Resistance to colistin can be explained by canonical mechanisms involving chromosomal mutations that activate lipid A modification pathways or by acquisition of plasmid-mediated mcr genes. These mechanisms modify the net charge of the bacterial outer membrane, reducing the binding affinity of colistin. However, an increasing number of genomic surveillance studies report colistin-resistant K. pneumoniae isolates that lack detectable alterations in known resistance mechanisms. This genotype-phenotype discordance suggests that additional regulatory mechanisms may contribute to colistin resistance. This review evaluates the hypothesis that mutation-independent regulatory changes within the PhoP/PhoQ-PmrA/PmrB-CrrA/CrrB signaling network may alter the output of lipid A modification pathways in isolates lacking detectable canonical resistance determinants. This model remains to be experimentally validated. The role of small regulatory RNAs (sRNAs) as potential post-transcriptional modulators of regulatory networks involved in envelope remodeling and antimicrobial susceptibility is explored as a potential explanation for this genotype-phenotype discordance. Finally, experimental approaches including transcriptomics, RNA-RNA interaction mapping, and functional validation are discussed as strategies to study sRNA-mediated regulatory networks. Understanding these regulatory mechanisms may help explain unresolved resistance phenotypes and refine antimicrobial resistance surveillance frameworks.

title: Central line-associated bloodstream infections outside the intensive care unit: Burden, pathogens, and antimicrobial susceptibility identified through a Victorian surveillance program
abstract: Prevention of central line-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI) is a priority in Australian intensive care units (ICUs). However, the epidemiology of CLABSI in non-ICU settings remains inadequately characterised, despite extensive use of central lines beyond the ICU. We aimed to determine CLABSI rates and microbiological aetiology in non-ICU wards and to compare these with corresponding ICU data from Victorian hospitals. CLABSI surveillance was undertaken voluntarily in non-ICU wards by Victorian health services between 2014 and 2025, utilising the Victorian Healthcare Associated Infection Surveillance System (VICNISS) CLABSI surveillance module, capturing CLABSI rates per 1000 central line days (CLD) as well as bloodstream infections related to mucosal barrier injury (MBI-BSI), in accordance with CDC/NHSN criteria. Retrospective analysis was performed to determine rates, pathogens, and antimicrobial susceptibility. Sixteen facilities participated in surveillance during the study period. 67 CLABSI events and 66,096 central line days were reported in non-ICU wards (predominantly haematology-oncology), corresponding to a CLABSI rate of 1.01 per 1000 CLD, which was significantly higher than the contemporaneous ICU CLABSI rate of 0.50 per 1000 CLD (IRR 3.13, 95% CI 1.88-5.22, p = 0.000). The most frequent pathogens responsible for non-ICU CLABSI were coagulase-negative Staphylococcus spp., Staphylococcus aureus, and Pseudomonas spp. A large burden of MBI-BSI events (n = 90) were also reported. CLABSI rates outside ICU are significantly higher than those reported in ICU settings. A substantial burden of CLABSI and MBI-BSI events were identified in haematology-oncology populations, supporting focused surveillance and infection prevention efforts in these high-risk cohorts.

title: Treatment variability among people assigned male at birth with repeat positive Mycoplasma genitalium tests: a case series
abstract: Mycoplasma genitalium (MG) can cause nongonococcal urethritis (NGU) and symptomatic proctitis. Rising antimicrobial resistance and lack of clinically available molecular resistance assays make MG treatment challenging. This study adds systematic data on the effectiveness of alternative MG regimens. Adult natal male patients who attended a public Sexual Health Clinic (SHC) and had ≥2 positive MG nucleic acid amplification tests within any 6-month period from January 2023-September 2025 were included. We classified cases as persistent infection or reinfection using clinical, demographic and self-reported behavioral data. For each patient, we summarized total number of visits, number, duration and components of each antibiotic regimen, and outcomes by MG clinical syndrome and infection status (persistence vs reinfection). Among 3,009 SHC patients, 400 (13%) had incident MG and 19 (4.8%) met inclusion criteria for repeat MG infection across 61 clinic visits. Nongonococcal urethritis (n=14/19 patients, 74%) and proctitis (n=2/19 patients, 10%) were the most prevalent syndromes. Suspected reinfection was common (40%). All 19 patients achieved cure, including 10 (53%) with microbiologic and 9 (47%) with presumed clinical cure, after treatment for a mean of 18-49 days with between 1-9 antibiotic regimens. Eight (53%) patients were cured with doxycycline plus moxifloxacin, two (100%) with doxycycline plus pristinamycin, three (75%) with minocycline alone, and three (75%) with prolonged minocycline plus tinidazole treatment. Despite frequent reinfection, most repeat positive tests represented persistent MG infections. All cases achieved cure after initial treatment failure, but many required multiple regimens over several weeks.

title: Pharmacological and Therapeutic Insights into Gepotidacin: A First-in-Class Triazaacenaphthylene Antibiotic
abstract: The growing challenge of antimicrobial resistance has necessitated the development of new antibiotics with novel mechanisms of action. Gepotidacin is a first-in-class triazaacenaphthylene antibiotic developed for the treatment of uncomplicated urinary tract infections (uUTIs) in female adults and adolescents. It inhibits bacterial DNA replication by targeting both DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV at a distinct binding site, differing from fluoroquinolones and therefore presenting a novel mechanism of action. However, resistance-associated mutations affecting susceptibility have been documented, emphasizing the need for ongoing monitoring. Pharmacokinetic studies indicate predictable, dose-dependent oral absorption suitable for twice- or thrice-daily dosing, with minimal accumulation and comparable profiles across populations. In terms of therapeutic success for the treatment of uUTIs, phase III clinical trials (EAGLE-2 and EAGLE-3) have demonstrated that gepotidacin was non‑inferior to the broad-spectrum antibiotic nitrofurantoin in EAGLE-2 and even superior to nitrofurantoin in EAGLE-3, with a tolerability profile comparable to other antibiotics of its class. Studies also suggest potential efficacy against uncomplicated gonorrhea (GC), including strains resistant to current therapies. Adverse events were generally mild to moderate, predominantly gastrointestinal, and caution is advised in patients with QT prolongation risk. While gepotidacin represents an important addition to the limited pool of oral antibiotics for these infections, its long-term clinical utility will depend on careful stewardship, resistance surveillance, and further evaluation in broader indications and combination regimens.

title: Simplified bacterial identification and antimicrobial resistance detection in bacteraemia by on-chip multiplexed LAMP from blood cultures
abstract: Bacteraemia is a severe infection associated with high risks of complications and mortality. Diagnosis relies mainly on blood cultures, followed by culture-based methods, which remain the gold-standard but are time-consuming. Isothermal bacterial DNA amplification provides a rapid, reliable and cost-effective alternative for identifying and characterising bacteria directly from positive blood cultures, enabling a timelier diagnosis, particularly in resources-limited settings. However, routine implementation has been hindered by sample processing requirements and its limited multiplexing capacity. Here, we developed an on-chip loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) workflow, ALADIM (accessible and integrated LAMP analysis for multiplex detection of infectious agents in microfluidics), that integrates bacterial extraction and multiplex LAMP, followed by instrument-free amplicons detection using lateral flow immunoassay (LFIA), all within two hours (24-48 hours for the gold-standard). To demonstrate the capabilities of our device, we targeted the most common bacteria found in bacteraemia,, the co-amplification of two highly prevalent antimicrobial resistance genes,and, and the detection of a positive control. Multiplex LAMP followed by LFIA detection was first evaluated using 14 strains cultured in LB. On-chip results were comparable to those obtained with our reference method (tube-based LAMP in a thermocycler followed by LFIA detection), showing 100% sensitivity, >84% specificity for the detection ofand, and 68% sensitivity, 83% specificity for. As a proof of concept for the applicability of the complete ALADIM workflow, we analysed positive overnight blood cultures spiked with 15 strains resulting in 61 independent experiments (DNA extraction/amplification/LFA readout). In this complex matrix, ALADIM specificity remained above 77% for all targets, while sensitivity exceeded 94% forandbut decreased to 56% for. A similar decrease in overall sensitivity was observed for the in-tube method (>68%), highlighting the challenges associated with direct whole-blood analysis. This feasibility study shows the integration of multiplex DNA amplification, microfluidic processing, and LFIA detection in a single platform. Future work will focus on improving sample preparation, assay performance in complex matrices, and expanding multiplexing capabilities of ALADIM towards additional targets, to deliver a clinically reliable point-of-care testing device for low- and middle-income countries.

title: Curcumin-based nanotherapeutics for colibacillosis in chickens: advances in veterinary microbiology
abstract: One of the most important bacterial agents of colibacillosis is Avian Pathogenic Escherichia coli (APEC), which affects the poultry industry by increasing mortality, reducing growth performance, and ultimately decreasing production efficiency. According the surveillance studies carried out in the European Union during the period of 2019-21, resistance to antibiotics has increased in E. coli due to transfer of genes between bacteria and humans. The rapid emergence of high antimicrobial resistance has accelerated research towards effective, natural, and antibiotic-free substitutes. Curcumin is a bioactive polyphenol extracted from Curcuma longa, has been widely studied for its antioxidant, immunomodulatory, antimicrobial, and anti-inflammatory properties. But, its use as a feed additive for chickens is limited because of the low bioavailability, rapid metabolism, and poor solubility. By applying nanotechnology techniques, researchers have successfully developed formulations that counteract these disadvantages and improve their bioavailability and stability. Curcumin nanoparticles work by causing damage to bacterial cell membrane, production of reactive oxygen species, and impeding bacterial cytokinesis by preventing the assembly of the FtsZ protein. Applications of nanoformulations of curcumin as a therapeutic agent for increasing the production of chicken, the various methods of delivering them to the birds, their pharmacokinetic studies and their effect on the growth performance of poultry birds have been critically and thoroughly analyzed in this review. Nanocurcumin at a concentration of 100 mg per kilogram of feed has demonstrated the best results for body weight gain, feed conversion ratio and feed intake. Despite the positive results, there are unsolved queries about the toxicokinetics, signaling molecular pathways, long-term safety, and dose standardization. For nanocurcumin to be logically incorporated into chicken health management, these obstacles must be overcome.

title: Pharmaceutical Pollution in India: Industrial Clustering, Environmental Hotspots, Antimicrobial Resistance, and Regulatory Gaps
abstract: Pharmaceutical pollution has emerged as a critical threat to environmental integrity and public health globally, with India occupying a uniquely prominent position as both the world's leading generic drug manufacturer and a major hotspot of active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) contamination. This review synthesizes current evidence on the distribution, magnitude, and health consequences of pharmaceutical pollution across India's principal manufacturing clusters and river systems, with particular emphasis on antimicrobial resistance (AMR) as a downstream public health consequence. Evidence environmental monitoring data, regulatory documentation, and case studies from Patancheru-Hyderabad (Telangana) and Baddi-Barotiwala-Nalagarh (Himachal Pradesh), we highlight evidence demonstrating that active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) in pharmaceutical manufacturing hotspots frequently occur at concentrations far exceeding recommended environmental thresholds, while also documenting the occurrence of hazardous heavy metals and organic solvents in affected environments. We further assess the regulatory landscape, including the Environment (Protection) Act (1986), Biomedical Waste Management Rules (2016), Zero Liquid Discharge mandates, and recent CPCB draft guidelines (2025), and identify persistent structural gaps in monitoring, enforcement, and compound-specific discharge standards. The review concludes with evidence-based recommendations for strengthening surveillance frameworks, integrating ecological risk quotient approaches, and aligning Indian policy with emerging international standards. Addressing pharmaceutical pollution is not merely an environmental imperative but an essential component of the global effort to contain AMR, protect vulnerable populations, and achieve health sustainability in low- and middle-income countries.

title: Performance evaluation of antimicrobial susceptibility testing devices across CLSI, EUCAST, ISO, FDA, and EMA frameworks: implications for breakpoint application
abstract: Broth microdilution (BMD) remains the reference standard for determining minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) in antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST). However, most routine laboratories rely on surrogate methods, including disk diffusion and commercial MIC-generating systems, whose results must correlate with those of reference BMD prior to clinical use. Evaluation criteria differ across standards development organizations (SDOs) and regulatory authorities, potentially affecting clinical interpretation, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). This mini-review compares evaluation frameworks from major SDOs-the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI), the European Committee on Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing (EUCAST), and the International Organization for Standardization (ISO)-and regulatory frameworks, including the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the EuropeanDiagnostic Regulation (IVDR). Key performance metrics, including essential agreement, categorical agreement, error rates, reproducibility, and bias, were analyzed, alongside differences in breakpoint setting and device approval pathways. Implications for clinical microbiology and antimicrobial stewardship were considered, with explicit emphasis on challenges faced in LMIC settings. Substantial heterogeneity exists across frameworks. CLSI and FDA emphasize breakpoint-dependent categorical agreement and error rates, whereas ISO prioritizes analytical measures such as essential agreement and bias without categorical errors. EUCAST broadly aligns with ISO analytically while separately maintaining responsibility for breakpoint setting. These differences can yield discordant device assessments, especially after breakpoint revisions. Surrogate MICs often correlate with BMD near breakpoints but may show systematic bias across MIC ranges, not fully captured by essential agreement alone, with important implications for LMIC laboratories. Divergent frameworks influence susceptibility interpretation, resistance surveillance, and antimicrobial stewardship, particularly in LMICs. Greater harmonization and awareness of methodological limitations are essential to ensure reliable AST reporting and support global antimicrobial resistance efforts across LMIC healthcare systems.

title: Anti-mycobacterial activity of phage-encoded lysterases
abstract: is a non-tuberculous(NTM) that is often associated with respiratory infections in persons with cystic fibrosis. High levels of antibiotic resistance makeinfections difficult to treat, highlighting the urgent need for alternative therapeutic strategies. Mycobacteriophage therapy-treatment of infections with viruses that infecthosts-shows considerable promise, but the narrow host specificity of the current mycobacteriophage repertoire limits this approach to personalized therapies. Here, we characterize the anti-.activity of mycobacteriophage-encoded Lysin B enzymes (lysterases). Lysterases are serine-esterases that cleave the ester bonds linking mycolic acids to either arabinogalactan or trehalose in the mycobacterial cell envelope to complete the lysis process. In this study, we explored their ability to kill a spectrum of clinically isolatedstrains when administered exogenously. Six phylogenetically distinct lysterases were purified, characterized on the surrogate, and their activity against a diverse panel of 24clinical strains was assessed. The enzymes exhibit a range of activities against these strains, but most have broad-spectrum activity with only minor variations among theisolates. However, the activities can be quite potent, resulting in up to six orders of magnitude of reduction in viability within 4 h with one activity unit of the enzymes, and act synergistically with amikacin. Overall, mycobacteriophage-encoded lysterases show considerable potential for antimycobacterial control, especially for topical applications.IMPORTANCEinfections are clinically challenging, and there is a high failure of resolvinginfections using antibiotics. Mycobacteriophages show promise in treatinginfections, but there is substantial variation among clinical isolates in their phage infection profiles. Mycobacteriophages are unusual in coding for lysis enzymes-lysterases-that target cell wall exposed constituents, and these can have potential antibacterial activity. Exploring the vast sequence diversity of thousands of phage-encoded lysterases identifies a subset that was expressed, purified, and tested for their ability to kill a broad range ofclinical strains. Lysterases with the broadest and greatest activity offer substantial potential for treatment ofinfection, especially where they display synergism with current antibiotics.

title: Draft genome sequences of four Helicobacter pylori isolates, from New Zealand
abstract: is a bacterium linked with gastric ulcers and gastric carcinoma that has high instances of antibiotic resistance. We present here the draft genome sequences of four.isolates, from four patients who had undergone gastroscopy and biopsies that were processed at Middlemore Hospital Laboratory, Auckland, New Zealand.

title: Last-line antimicrobial resistance genes in food-chain Enterococcus faecium sensu stricto: a 2,090-genome public-archive audit with whole-genome species validation
abstract: The extent to which food-chain bacteria carry last-line antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) is poorly quantified. We screened 2,090 NCBI genomes whose BioSample metadata indicated food-chain association. Mash-based validation against type strains reassigned 663 genomes (31.7%) to Enterococcus lactis (former clade B) and exposed one misidentified record; a standardized minimap2/ResFinder re-screen removed three annotation-based false-positive calls. The primary estimand was the proportion of last-line ARG (vanA, optrA, poxtA, cfr)-positive genomes within this predefined sampling frame, not population prevalence. After excluding apparent clinical admixture, 140/1,283 E. faecium sensu stricto genomes (10.91%; 95% CI 9.32-12.74) carried a last-line ARG, versus 4/646 E. lactis (0.62%; 0.24-1.58). vanA carriage concentrated in clonal complex CC17 (59/83 observed carriers), whereas optrA/poxtA carriage did not (20-28% CC17). Carriage rose from 4.8% (2013-16) to 13.1% (2021-26) among dated genomes while multi-ARG carriage declined. No carrier had measured susceptibility data; findings are genomic and archive-bound.

title: Development and Application of a Rapid 23S rRNA-Targeted Reverse Transcription Quantitative PCR System for the Detection and Quantification of Enterobacterales
abstract: Bacteria belonging to the family Enterobacteriaceae occur as commensals or pathogens in humans. The increasing prevalence of multidrug-resistant bacteria has raised global concern. Following the reclassification of Enterobacteriaceae species into the order Enterobacterales in 2016. However, no quantification method has been reported that is designed and validated in the context of the current order-level taxonomy of Enterobacterales. Therefore, we aimed to develop a novel reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) system for the quantification of Enterobacterales based on 23S rRNA. The system was used to quantify Enterobacterales species, and its applicability was evaluated using fecal samples from 99 patients with gastrointestinal cancer and 10 healthy volunteers. Furthermore, we performed a proof-of-concept evaluation of its utility for rapid assessment of antimicrobial susceptibility in carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE). The system exhibited high analytical sensitivity and enabled quantification of diverse Enterobacterales spp., including newly classified species, with theoretical detection limits of 10cells/g feces and 1 cell/mL blood. In healthy volunteers, intestinal Enterobacterales were dominated by Escherichia coli and Enterobacter, whereas preoperative patients with gastrointestinal cancer exhibited greater diversity. In vitro, viable CRE cell counts determined by the RT-qPCR system 2 h after antibiotic treatment correlated well with culture-based susceptibility results obtained after 24 h, suggesting the feasibility of rapid antimicrobial susceptibility assessment within 6 h. The developed 23S rRNA RT-qPCR system provides a sensitive approach for quantifying Enterobacterales within the current taxonomic framework and may facilitate the rapid assessment of antimicrobial activity against CRE. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: There is no clinical trial registration.

title: Genomic diversity of human-associated Mycobacterium bovis in Canada
abstract: Human infections caused byin Canada are not well documented. The following study analyzed(excluding BCG) isolates identified in public health laboratories across Canadian provinces between 2000 and 2025. Whole-genome sequencing was used to catalog mutations linked to antimicrobial resistance and evaluate the genomic relatedness of isolates. The majority of samples in this study were non-respiratory (60%). Of 74 study isolates, 69 (93%) were phenotypically sensitive to first-line drugs isoniazid, rifampin, and ethambutol. The most frequently encounteredclusters belonged tocomplex lineages La 1.7 and La 1.8. Although some isolates showed phylogenetic clustering, their lack of spatial and temporal relatedness suggested sporadic cases rather than localtransmission. Of all first-line drugs evaluated, isoniazid showed the lowest concordance (94.4%) between phenotypic and genotypic methods. The isolates in this study harbor some mutations that are not currently documented in the WHO mutation catalog, indicating that these variants may be rare. The findings suggest that the prevalence ofinfection in Canada is low with cases unlikely to be acquired through human-to-human transmission.IMPORTANCEIncidence of human infections due toin Canada is largely unknown as these data are not collected or annually published. This research is a first effort to identify historicalisolates that were available for culture, had drug susceptibility testing data, and were analyzed through whole-genome sequencing. The annual reporting of these data in Canada holds value.

title: Efficacy of minocycline-containing bismuth quadruple therapy for Helicobacter pylori infection: a single-center retrospective study
abstract: Increasing antibiotic resistance has undermined Helicobacter pylori eradication. Despite a low resistance to minocycline, clinical evidence for minocycline-containing bismuth quadruple therapy (MCQT) limited. This retrospective study aimed to evaluate the clinical efficacy of MCQT. Patients who had Helicobacter pylori infection byC-urea breath testing at our department from October 2024 to July 2025 were screened. They were classified into MCQT (minocycline-amoxicillin-acid-inhibitors-bismuth [MAAB], minocycline-clarithromycin-acid-inhibitors-bismuth [MCAB], and minocycline-levofloxacin-acid-inhibitors-bismuth [MLAB]) and non-MCQT (amoxicillin-clarithromycin-acid-inhibitors-bismuth [ACAB] and amoxicillin-levofloxacin-acid-inhibitors-bismuth [ALAB]). Four comparisons (MAAB vs. ACAB, MCAB vs. ACAB, MLAB vs. ALAB, and MAAB vs. ALAB) were separately performed in treatment‑naïve and treatment‑experienced patients. Logistic regression analyses were used to identify the influence factors. Overall, 687 treatment-naïve and 92 treatment-experienced Helicobacter pylori patients were included. MAAB demonstrated significantly higher eradication rates than ACAB in both groups (P = 0.020, P = 0.016), with no significant differences in other comparisons. Multivariate logistic regression analysis indicated that female was independently associated with a higher eradication rate in treatment-naïve patients in three comparisons (MAAB vs. ACAB, P = 0.021; MCAB vs. ACAB, P = 0.009; MAAB vs. ALAB, P = 0.043). MCQT achieve favorable Helicobacter pylori eradication rates in both treatment-naïve and treatment-experienced patients, and MAAB demonstrates a significantly higher eradication rate than ACAB.

title: Improving hand hygiene compliance in Greek hospitals: results of a Nationwide Quality Improvement Program (GRIPP-SNF)
abstract: Hand hygiene (HH) is the most effective way to prevent healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) and the spread of antimicrobial-resistant pathogens. HH compliance is particularly relevant in Greece, which has among the highest rates of HAIs and antimicrobial resistance in the European Union. The aim of our study was to assess current HH practices in Greece and to improve compliance. Prospective observational quasi-experimental (before-after) study. Eight public adult tertiary hospitals. "Physicians, Nurses, and Ancillary Healthcare Workers." Three time periods were defined: the baseline period (December 2021-June 2022), intervention period (July 2022-January 2023), and postintervention period (February 2023-May 2024). An improvement bundle was implemented. A minimum of 30 observations per department per month of HH opportunities were required. Trained observers conducted observations using a standardized data collection tool. Interrupted time-series analysis was performed. 38,069 HH opportunities were observed. Overall compliance was 48.5%. Glove use without proper HH was observed in 72.9% of opportunities. Alcohol-based hand rub was used for HH by 57.8% of HCW who conducted HH. Compliance improved from 37.3% in the baseline period to 53.3% after the intervention (16% increase,< .001). Improved compliance was observed in 9/13 (69%) intensive care units. Of 10 participating medical and surgical wards, improved compliance was observed in 9 (90%) units, and improvement ranged from 7.2% to 28.3. Overall, we found low compliance rates and gaps in HH practices in Greek hospitals. A quality improvement intervention improved overall HH compliance. This is the largest study of HH compliance in Greek hospitals to date.

title: Acne: epidemiology, risk factors, pathogenesis, management and cutting-edge research
abstract: Acne vulgaris is a widespread chronic inflammatory skin condition particularly affecting the pilosebaceous unit, with its pathogenesis intricately linked to excessive sebum production, abnormal follicular keratinization, overcolonization by Cutibacterium acnes (C. acnes), and dysregulated host immune responses. Beyond its dermatological manifestations, the disorder is frequently associated with psychological comorbidities such as anxiety and depression, significantly impacting patients' quality of life. A genetic predisposition is evident, with associated polymorphisms involving pathways related to sebaceous gland activity, inflammatory regulation, and hormonal metabolism. Interactions among immune cells, including macrophages and dendritic cells, along with underlying molecular mechanisms, further contribute to its pathogenesis. Conventional acne treatments face challenges such as increasing antibiotic resistance and limited patient adherence. As a result, clinical research and practice are increasingly focusing on targeted, mechanism-based precision strategies. Recent advances in targeted biologics and vaccines directed against C. acnes have demonstrated promise in clinical studies, offering new avenues for acne management. This review provides a systematic overview of the epidemiology, risk factors, diagnostic classifications, and comorbidities associated with acne, with a particular focus on contemporary insights into its immunopathogenesis and molecular mechanisms. Additionally, it synthesizes current treatment modalities and explores emerging directions, such as acne vaccines and biologics, to serve as a reference for further mechanistic investigation and therapeutic advancement.

title: From Rare to Rising: A Story of Enterobacter-associated Pneumonia Evolving in the Community
abstract: Pneumonia is a common cause of mortality and morbidity worldwide and is the fifth leading cause of death. It is generally caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and some atypical microorganisms. Interestingly, a member of ESKAPE pathogens, mainly Enterobacter cloacae complex, is increasingly showing its presence in the samples of lower respiratory tract specimens. Emergence of multidrug resistance (MDR) in these bacteria, including resistance to last-resort carbapenems, has led to an increased interest in this organism causing pneumonia. (1) Prevalence of E. cloacae complex among community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) patients and (2) antibiotic resistance pattern of these pathogens. Respiratory samples from adult patients were processed according to standard microbiological techniques, including direct smear examination, incubation in blood, MacConkey and chocolate agar plates, and Gram staining. Identification of E. cloacae complex and antibiotic susceptibility testing, along with resistance patterns, was performed by automated ID/AST instrument. About 15.7% of E. cloacae complex-associated CAP patients were found over a 1-year study period. Antimicrobial susceptibility tests indicated a MDR profile in 58.3% of isolates. Resistance was mostly to carbapenems (72.73%), followed by aztreonam (69.7%), piperacillin-tazobactam (68%), and fluoroquinolones (63.6%). E. cloacae complex is an emerging and clinically significant pathogen causing CAP. Its MDR profile contributes to an increased tendency to intensive care unit admission and the development of sepsis. Hence, detecting this pathogen in lower respiratory tract specimens should be treated as a high alert and should prompt treatment at the earliest.

title: Antioxidant-producing extremophile regulates gut microbiota of black soldier fly larvae to inhibit conjugative transfer mediated by plasmids in municipal sludge
abstract: Oxidative stress induced by heavy metals and antibiotics in municipal sludge inhibits the gut development of black soldier fly larvae (BSFL), compromising pollutant-processing capacity of their gut microbiota. Herein, Deinococcus radiodurans was colonized into the BSFL gut and established an antioxidant cascade regulatory system in concert with the gut microbiota, synergistically reducing the enrichment of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) in municipal sludge. Results showed that bioaugmentation with Deinococcus radiodurans scavenges reactive oxygen species and upregulates the expression of G-protein and s14e genes in BSFL gut, maintaining normal gut function. On this basis, we propose two potential mechanisms responsible for inhibiting the horizontal transfer of ARGs (HGT). At the molecular level, bioaugmentation reduces environmental co-selection pressure through heavy metal immobilization mediated by extracellular polymeric substances and SlpA protein, as well as antibiotic degradation driven by gut microbiota, reducing the abundances of the class 1 integron integrase gene (intI1), conjugative transfer gene (traG), and ARGs (aphA and tetA) in municipal sludge by more than one order of magnitude. At the ecological level, bioaugmentation reshapes the microbial community structure of sludge, reducing the abundance of Pseudomonadota carrying mobile genetic elements and ARGs by approximately 26%. Moreover, bioaugmentation disrupted the co-occurrence of the mer operon and ARGs (sul1). Conjugative experiments revealed that co-cultivation with Deinococcus radiodurans reduced the conjugative transfer frequency of the ARG-carrying RP4 plasmid by 91%. Therefore, this study elucidates how antioxidant-producing extremophiles can strengthen BSFL system to inhibit HGT and reduce ARG enrichment.

title: Trends towards multidrug-resistant bacteria: heterocyclic compounds containing antimicrobial agents: review
abstract: The rapid emergence of multidrug-resistant (MDR) pathogens poses a severe global health threat, as current antibiotics become increasingly ineffective due to antimicrobial resistance (AMR), irrational drug use across human, veterinary, and agricultural sectors, and aggressive pharmaceutical marketing. This crisis is further aggravated by a shortage of novel antibacterial agents entering clinical practice, highlighting the urgent need for new treatment modalities and drug repurposing strategies. In response, heterocyclic compounds have emerged as a highly versatile and promising class of organic molecules with unique broad-spectrum antibacterial activity against both Gram-positive and Gram-negative strains. To successfully translate these bench discoveries into clinical solutions against superbugs, a combined approach integrating rigorous antibiotic stewardship principles with streamlined regulatory pathways is essential.

title: Efficacy of Ccombody as an Immunoprophylaxis Strategy: Impact on Immune Gene Expression of Pacific White Shrimp (Penaeus vannamei) Against Acute Hepatopancreatic Necrosis Disease (AHPND)
abstract: Acute hepatopancreatic necrosis disease (AHPND) is caused by a plasmid bearing strain of Vibrio parahaemolyticus (Vp), which produces PirA and PirB toxins that specifically target and damage hepatopancreatic and epithelial cells of the shrimp gastrointestinal tract. The impact of AHPND, together with concerns regarding antibiotic resistance, has necessitated investigations into alternative forms of disease prevention. This study evaluated the protective efficacy of Ccombody, a recombinant variable lymphocyte receptor B (VLRB)-based antibody targeting the PirA toxin, on immune-related gene expression and survival in Pacific white shrimp (Penaeus vannamei) challenged with Vp. Shrimp were allocated into six experimental groups, each in triplicate. Two groups served as controls fed a basal commercial diet: an unchallenged negative control and a Vp-challenged positive control. An additional reference group was fed a commercial diet supplemented with IgY at 500 mg/100 g feed. The remaining three treatment groups were fed diets supplemented with the Ccombody at 1, 10 or 100 mg/100 g feed for 7 days. At 7 days post-feeding (7 d.p.f.), prophenoloxidase-2 (proPO-2), anti-lipopolysaccharide factors-1 (ALF-1) and penaeidin-4 (PEN4) expression levels showed no significant differences among treatments. At 24 h post-infection (24 h.p.i.), proPO-2 expression of Ccombody groups differed significantly from both the positive and negative control groups (p < 0.05), while no significant differences were observed among Ccombody-treated groups. ALF-1 expression remained unchanged across treatments. In contrast, the Ccombody 1 and 10 mg/100 g feed groups showed significantly enhanced PEN4 expression compared to the positive control group (p < 0.05). Notably, PEN4 expression significantly increased in Ccombody 1 mg/100 g feed group at 24 h.p.i. relative to 7 d.p.f. (p < 0.05), whereas a decline was observed in the positive control and Ig-Guard A groups. Principal component analysis (PCA) also showed the same scattering trend towards gene expression analysis at both 7 d.p.f. and 24 h.p.i. Dietary supplementation with Ccombody 1, 10 and 100 mg/100 g feed effectively reduced the mortality rate following challenge with V. parahaemolyticus causing AHPND. All supplemented groups showed highly significant reduction in mortality compared to the positive control group (p < 0.001). Among them, the 10 and 100 mg/100 g feed groups exhibited the lowest mortality rates (3.70% ± 1.28% and 3.70% ± 3.39%, respectively). When considered alongside the immune-related gene expression, these findings suggest that Ccombody has strong potential as an alternative immunoprophylaxis strategy for the prevention of Vp.

title: Dual-Pathogen Defense: Engineering an ExPEC Ghost to Display Protective Epitopes of Streptococcus suis
abstract: Streptococcus suis and extraintestinal pathogenic Escherichia coli (ExPEC) cause severe swine infections and major economic losses worldwide. Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) and polymicrobial interactions complicate disease control. Existing vaccine strategies are insufficient to provide broad cross-serotype protection against S. suis strains while simultaneously combating ExPEC infections. We developed a bivalent vaccine platform that integrates bacterial ghost (BG) technology with surface antigen display. By utilizing the porcine ExPEC strain PU-1 as a carrier, which could cause acute sepsis in mouse infection model. Using an Lpp'-OmpA surface display system, we constructed recombinant BGs derived from E. coli that express a multi-epitope antigen against S. suis (MEAS 1), while retaining native E. coli antigenic components as the immunogen against ExPEC. Administration of this vaccine induced robust cellular and humoral immune responses specific to both S. suis and E. coli. The vaccine demonstrated dual protection: 70%-90% survival against S. suis (serotypes 2/9) and 70% against ExPEC challenge in mouse model. Porcine trials demonstrated a significant reduction in bacteremia and provided effective protection against pathogenic challenges. This platform offers a potential solution for preventing infections caused by S. suis and ExPEC.

title: Efflux modulation as an antimicrobial strategy: mechanisms and translational perspectives
authors: da Cruz Nizer WS et al.
abstract: Efflux pumps are widely viewed as antibiotic resistance determinants, yet their roles in stress adaptation, virulence, quorum sensing, and biofilm formation make them context-dependent therapeutic targets. This Perspective distinguishes four efflux intervention strategies: direct inhibition, bioenergetic or membrane-mediated suppression, regulatory modulation, and dual-effect approaches. We examine why promising in vitro findings rarely translate clinically and argue that efflux-targeting strategies require defined therapeutic objectives and integrated multidisciplinary approaches.

title: Application of food waste digestates and digestate-derived biochar for mitigating antibiotic, Pb, and ARGs pollution in soil containing biodegradable microplastics: The key role of exogenous dissolved organic carbon and organic nitrogen
abstract: The widespread use of biodegradable plastic mulch films and organic manure in agriculture has led to the accumulation of biodegradable microplastics (BMPs), heavy metals, and antibiotics in soil. In this study, three food waste-derived soil amendments, including digestion liquid (DL), digested food waste (DFW), and DFW-derived biochar (DFW-BC), were evaluated for their ability to mitigate co-pollution of Pb, sulfamethazine (SM2), and antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) in soil containing poly(butylene succinate) microplastics (PBS-MPs). All amendments enhanced SM2 dissipation, and DFW and DFW-BC facilitated the transformation of acid-soluble Pb into less mobile fractions, whereas DL exhibited a more modest effect on Pb immobilization. Regarding ARGs, DL amendment reduced the relative abundances of intl1 and sul1 by 21.6% and 35.0%, respectively. DFW amendment achieved reductions of 77.6% for intl1 and 57.1% for sul2, while DFW-BC amendment reduced them by 17.8% and 28.6%, respectively. Correlation network analysis suggested that Bacillaceae was identified as a potential host of sul1 and intl1, whereas sul2 potential hosts mainly belonged to the phylum Proteobacteria. Mechanistically, these amendments primarily drove changes in the soil bacterial community by increasing soil dissolved organic matter (DOM) and total dissolved nitrogen (TDN) contents, while reducing water-soluble SM2 concentration, thereby suppressing the proliferation of potential ARGs hosts such as Bacillaceae and mitigating soil ARGs contamination. This study demonstrates that food waste-derived amendments, as value-added reutilization resources, offer a promising strategy for the remediation of soils co-contaminated with BMPs and multiple pollutants.

title: Pollutant-ARG associations show contrasting hydrometeorological context dependence at aggregate and resistance-class levels
abstract: Riverine antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) are commonly interpreted in relation to pollutant concentrations, but these associations may also depend on hydrometeorological context and the resolution at which ARG responses are analyzed. We integrated ARG and pollutant datasets from the Pearl and Xiangjiang rivers with campaign-window precipitation, air temperature and streamflow data to compare pollutant-state, hydrometeorological and combined explanations of total and class-specific ARG variation. At the total-ARG level, pollutant-state gradients captured most of the coherent explainable variation, whereas hydrometeorological variables alone contributed relatively little. At the resistance-class level, supported model assignments were concentrated mainly in pollutant-state and combined models, with little support for hydrometeorology-only models. No interaction between pollutant-state variables and hydrometeorological conditions was retained for total ARG abundance after FDR correction in either basin. In contrast, multiple FDR-retained interactions were identified among resistance classes, with streamflow-related modifiers occurring more frequently than meteorological modifiers in the primary analysis. However, none of these class-level interactions met all evaluated robustness criteria, and their number and identity were sensitive to response specification. These findings should therefore be interpreted as exploratory signals rather than evidence of causal effect modification. These patterns indicate that hydrometeorological context was associated with variation in pollutant-ARG relationships at finer response resolution. Taken together, the contrasting patterns between aggregate and class-specific responses suggest that aggregation may provide less information about heterogeneous context dependence, although the underlying mechanisms remain unresolved. Overall, pollutant-state gradients characterized the aggregate ARG signal, whereas hydrometeorological context was more apparent in class-specific associations.

title: Association of cirA allelic variation with cefiderocol susceptibility and virulence-associated lineages in Klebsiella pneumoniae
abstract: Klebsiella pneumoniae comprises multidrug-resistant and hypervirulent lineages, and cefiderocol uptake may partly depend on iron transport receptors such as CirA. However, the clinical distribution and phenotypic relevance of cirA alleles remain unclear. To determine whether cirA allelic variation is associated with cefiderocol susceptibility and virulence-related traits in clinical K. pneumoniae isolates. We analysed 480 non-duplicate clinical isolates for cirA allele, sequence type, capsular locus, β-lactamase genes, cefiderocol MICs by broth microdilution in iron-depleted cation-adjusted Mueller-Hinton broth, siderophore production, virulence score and Galleria mellonella lethality. Five major cirA allelic groups were identified. cirA198 was associated with higher cefiderocol MIC distributions and included all cefiderocol-resistant isolates, which also carried bla, blaand bla, indicating multifactorial reduced susceptibility. In contrast, cirA1 was linked to ST23-KL1 isolates and was associated with higher virulence scores, increased siderophore production and greater lethality in G. mellonella. Major cirA alleles are associated with distinct K. pneumoniae clonal backgrounds: cirA198 with ST11-KL64 multidrug-resistant isolates and elevated cefiderocol MICs, and cirA1 with ST23-KL1 hypervirulence-associated traits. cirA allelic typing may serve as a lineage-associated marker, although isogenic studies are needed to define independent causal roles.

title: Unravelling the antimicrobial mechanism of chitosan: A structure-function approach
abstract: Chitosan (CS) has emerged as a promising alternative against antimicrobial resistance due to its broad-spectrum antimicrobial properties. CS's antimicrobial activity is supposed to be influenced by its molecular weight, degree of deacetylation, chemical functionalization, and biological origin. Despite extensive research, the mechanisms underlying its bioactivity remain poorly understood, with hypotheses including membrane disruption, ion chelation, and intracellular interference. In this study, we systematically evaluated the antimicrobial efficacy and mechanisms of action of various CS samples having different molecular weight (from 2 to 300 kDa), different functionalization (carboxyl and lactate moieties) or different origin (from crustacean or fungal source). Through various chemical and microbiological assays, we identify the most effective structural features leading to the highest performance and its mechanism of action, corresponding to lactate-functionalised CS. Similarly, 7 kDa CS displays the best activity among pristine CS with different MWs. This systematic analysis offers valuable insights for the rational design of more efficient, sustainable CS-based antimicrobial therapies, contributing to developing alternative strategies against microbial infections.

title: Evolution of Bacterial Yield and Antimicrobial Resistance in Chronic Rhinosinusitis Patients in a Dedicated Sinus Centre
abstract: Antibiotics are frequently prescribed for acute exacerbations of chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS). However, antimicrobial resistance presents a challenge for the ongoing and future management of CRS patients. This study aims to examine the current and past microbiological yield and antimicrobial resistance profile in a tertiary sinus centre. A retrospective results review for the calendar years from 2015 to 2018 and 2019 to 2024 was conducted on all CRS patients who had sinonasal microbiological samples taken during their outpatient visits with a history of previous endoscopic sinus surgery (ESS). A total of 706 cultures were analysed from 338 patients. Clinically significant organisms were identified in 60.0% of cases in 2015-2018 and 71.9% of cases in 2019-2024 (p = 0.003). Whilst Staphylococcus aureus remained the predominant isolate in both groups, Gram-negative organisms rose significantly (32.9%-46.5%, p = 0.004), particularly non-Pseudomonas and Enterobacteriaceae species. Interestingly, classical acute bacterial rhinosinusitis pathogens (Staphylococcus pneumoniae, Moraxella catarrhalis, Haemophilus influenzae) were detected in only 28.0% and 23.8% of cases in the respective study periods. Resistance to clarithromycin in S. aureus isolates increased significantly from 12.1% to 27.5% (p = 0.0008), whilst resistance to doxycycline and amoxicillin also rose, though these changes were not statistically significant. Resistance to co-amoxiclav increased from 0.3% to 3.2% in 2019-2024. (p = 0.0276). There has been an increase in the incidence of Gram-negative bacteria as well as antibiotic resistance in CRS sinonasal cultures. These findings emphasise the importance of endoscopically guided cultures and culture-directed antibiotic therapy when managing postoperative CRS exacerbations.

title: Single-cell transcriptomic atlas uncovers Immune/Structural lineage remodeling and fibrosis in Klebsiella pneumoniae-infected porcine lungs
abstract: (KP) is a predominant pathogen in respiratory infections, whose widespread antibiotic resistance poses severe public health risks and economic burdens. As the primary target of KP infection, the lung contains diverse immune cells, while pulmonary cellular responses to KP remain poorly understood. This study integrated single-cell RNA sequencing, flow cytometry, RT-qPCR, and immunofluorescence to investigate porcine lung cell response from healthy pigs and those infected with multidrug-resistant, highly-virulent KP. Post-infection, myeloid cells (neutrophils, monocytes, and interstitial macrophages) were rapidly activated with upregulated signatures related to neutrophil migration and interferon production. Alveolar macrophages (AM) exhibited marked heterogeneity: KP infection was associated with apoptosis in proliferating, monocyte-derived, and tissue-resident AM subsets, indicating a disruption of homeostasis, while infection-specific subsets (AM_MHCII, AM_CXCL2) displayed enhanced antigen presentation, inflammatory activity, and pro-fibrotic potential. Under homeostasis, γδ T and CD8ααT cells were the predominant T cell populations. After infection, CX3CR1CD8ααT cells were activated, and CD8γδ T cells increased their interactions with myeloid cells, predominantly through ligand-receptor pairs such as TNF-TNFRSF1B and IFNG-IFNGR1/2. Furthermore, KP induced lung fibroblast proliferation and activation via the ROS-mediated TGF-β/SMAD pathway, WNT pathway, and aerobic glycolysis. Concurrently, infection reduced the proportion of ATII and transitional AT0 cells, which may impair their differentiation into ATI cells and compromise epithelial barrier function. Thus, this study is the first to characterize the dynamics of KP infection in porcine lungs at single-cell resolution. It advances our understanding of KP-host interactions, and provides a framework for anti-KP therapeutic development.

title: Comparative study of antibiotic resistance and virulence profiles of exoU and exoS Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolates from urinary tract infections and microbial keratitis in Bangladesh and India
abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an important opportunistic pathogen in urinary tract infections (UTIs) and microbial keratitis (MK), but differences in resistance and virulence between exoU and exoS P. aeruginosa isolates across regions and infection sites remain poorly understood. This study compared antibiotic resistance and virulence profiles of exoU and exoS P. aeruginosa isolates from Bangladeshi and Indian UTIs, and from Indian UTIs and MK collections. A total of 23 Bangladeshi UTI isolates were analyzed by broth microdilution for susceptibility to ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, gentamicin, and tobramycin, and by whole-genome sequencing (WGS) to identify resistance-associated mutations, acquired resistance genes, and virulence factors. These WGS data were compared with 15 publicly available Indian UTI genomes, while the Indian UTI genomes were compared with 19 publicly available Indian MK genomes. In the Bangladeshi UTI cohort, exoU isolates showed greater resistance to fluoroquinolones and aminoglycosides than exoS isolates. Comparative analysis of Bangladeshi versus Indian UTI isolates and Indian UTI versus MK isolates showed that exoU isolates carried a burden of resistance mutations, including enrichment of GyrA Thr83Ile, ParE Asp533Glu, MexR Val126Glu, MexB Ser1041Glu, and MexC Ala262Glu. Aminoglycoside-associated substitutions FusA2 Gln161Leu and ParR Leu153Arg and Ser170Asn were more common in exoU UTI isolates. Acquired resistance genes showed aac(6')-II and aac(3)-Id were linked to Bangladeshi UTI, rmtF associated with Indian UTI, and crpP confined to MK exoU isolates. Virulence profiling showed exoU enrichment in pldA, pvdY, and csrA, whereas exoS was associated with pilC, pilV, pilW, pilY2, and pilA. Collectively, these results indicate that exoU and exoS isolates differ in both their resistance and virulence profiles, while also showing evidence of geographic and infection-site-specific adaptation.

title: Comparative genomics of hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates from Brazil
abstract: Klebsiella pneumoniae represents a major public health threat at the convergence of antimicrobial resistance and hypervirulence. While classical K. pneumoniae (cKp) is a leading cause of healthcare-associated infections, hypervirulent K. pneumoniae (hvKp) causes severe invasive disease in otherwise healthy individuals. We performed a comparative genomic analysis of hvKp (n = 8) and cKp (n = 17) isolates recovered in Salvador, Brazil. The eight Brazilian hvKp isolates displayed the canonical hypervirulence genotype, encoding the five major biomarkers (iroB, iucA, peg-344, rmpA, and rmpA2) while carrying only a limited repertoire of intrinsic antimicrobial resistance genes. These isolates belonged to sequence types ST23, ST65, ST86, ST3690, and ST5750 and were associated with K1 or K2 capsular types and the O1 antigen. In three isolates, iroB was detected in both chromosomal and plasmid-associated regions, a dual localization reported at low frequency among hvKp. The predominant plasmid replicons were IncHI1B (pNDM-MAR) and repB_KLEB, with IncFIB (K) in two isolates. Screening for mobile genetic elements recovered an F-type conjugative transfer locus in these two isolates only. Chromosomes and plasmids showed high similarity with well-characterized reference hvKp strains, including SGH10 and NTUH-K2044, as well as the pLVPK virulence plasmid. Comparative proteomics analysis identified 53 protein clusters conserved across hvKp strains examined. Among these were four hypothetical proteins previously associated with invasive liver infection, containing DUF1471, DUF417, and carboxymuconolactone decarboxylase-related domains, suggesting potential roles in pathogenicity. Collectively, these findings expand current knowledge of hvKp genetic diversity in Salvador, Brazil and highlight genomic features that may contribute to the emergence and maintenance of the hypervirulent phenotype.

title: Comparison of antimicrobial susceptibility testing methods for aztreonam-avibactam against NDM-producing Enterobacterales clinical isolates
abstract: Aztreonam-avibactam (ATM-AVI) is a promising therapeutic for New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase-producing Enterobacterales (NDM-E) infections. We evaluated the performance of disk diffusion and gradient diffusion methods compared with reference broth microdilution (BMD) for ATM-AVI susceptibility testing. A total of 245 non-duplicate NDM-E isolates were included, collected from unique patients at hospitals in Chile and the United States between 2022 and 2024. Nine ATM-AVI non-susceptible isolates from a separate collection were added to enrich for resistant isolates, yielding a total of 254 isolates. Reference BMD was performed according to Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) criteria. ATM-AVI disk diffusion and two gradient diffusion methods (ETEST and MIC Test Strip) were evaluated against BMD using categorical agreement, essential agreement, and CLSI-defined error rates. All 245 NDM-E isolates were susceptible to ATM-AVI (MIC ≤4/4 µg/mL), with MIC₅₀/₉₀ values of 0.25/4 and 1/4 µg/mL, respectively. The collection consisted of(71%),complex (21%), and(8%). Predominant NDM alleles includedand. Disk diffusion demonstrated 98% categorical agreement (250/254), with four minor errors. Both gradient diffusion methods achieved 99% categorical agreement (252/254), with no very major or major errors and two minor errors. Essential agreement was 67% for ETEST and 85% for MIC Test Strip; both methods tended to underestimate ATM-AVI MICs relative to BMD. ATM-AVI demonstrated robustactivity against a contemporary NDM-E cohort. Disk and gradient diffusion methods are practical alternatives to BMD for clinical laboratories.

title: Adaptive landscape of the metallo-β-lactamase NDM-1 to emerging β-lactam-based therapies
abstract: The New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase (NDM) is a major determinant of carbapenem resistance. This has prompted the development of novel therapeutic strategies to treat NDM producers. Since these therapies impose new selective pressures, their clinical deployment may favor NDM variants carrying escape mutations. To anticipate these events and inform therapeutic decisions, we explored the evolutionary landscape of NDM-1 under different selective constraints. To this end, we generated a diverse library ofvariants and challenged it with zinc starvation, antibiotics, or β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combinations that represent novel and emerging therapies. Selection under zinc limitation and cefotaxime identified mutational trajectories that recapitulate clinical NDM evolution, validating the diversity of the library and its predictive nature. Drug-specific selections revealed sharply different evolutionary pathways. Mecillinam selected a narrow evolutionary pathway centered on residues N220 and M67, which enhance productive active-site interactions with this penicillin. Cefepime/taniborbactam selected multiple escape routes, dominated by substitutions at E152 and, secondarily, K211, that impair productive interaction with taniborbactam. In contrast, cefiderocol/xeruborbactam under iron-depleted conditions and aztreonam/avibactam did not select NDM variants conferring an improved resistance phenotype in the testedbackground. These results show that NDM evolution is constrained by the chemistry of each therapeutic challenge. Substrate adaptation is possible for mecillinam, inhibitor escape is readily accessible for taniborbactam, whereas no NDM-centered escape was detected for the aztreonam- and xeruborbactam-based conditions tested. Mapping drug-specific NDM-centered landscapes can identify therapies that readily select enzyme-level escape and those for which resistance is more likely to require mechanisms beyondsequence variation.IMPORTANCECarbapenem-resistant infections by Enterobacterales are increasingly difficult to treat because bacteria can destroy some of the most powerful antibiotics used in the clinic. This study focuses oncarrying variants of the New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase (NDM), an enzyme that enables bacteria to resist carbapenem antibiotics. New therapies are being developed to overcome this problem, but bacteria may evolve again when exposed to these treatments. Here, we tested how New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase can adapt under the evolutionary pressure of last-resort therapies. The results show that not all treatments carry the same evolutionary risk. Some drugs allow the enzyme to adapt through specific mutations, whereas other combinations did not yield improved NDM variants in the tested bacterial background. This work identifies which treatments readily select changes within NDM and which may require resistance mechanisms elsewhere in the bacterial cell. These findings should be integrated with host species, permeability, drug targets, metal uptake, and co-produced enzymes when considering clinical resistance.

title: A global atlas of the gut virome reveals subtype-specific and functional alterations in irritable bowel syndrome
abstract: The gut virome is a critical component of the microbiome-gut-brain axis; however, its role in irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) remains poorly understood due to limited sample sizes and geographic bias. We aimed to construct a comprehensive global atlas of the IBS gut virome to elucidate its composition, functional potential, and clinical relevance across diverse populations and IBS subtypes. We integrated multi-cohort data comprising 1,104 samples (790 IBS patients and 314 healthy controls) from 11 cohorts across 10 geographic regions. A standardized bioinformatic pipeline was employed to perform viral mining from metagenomic and virus-like particle-enriched metaviromic data. The IBS virome exhibited significant taxonomic alterations, with specific viral signatures distinguishing IBS-D, IBS-C, and IBS-M subtypes. Geographic region was identified as a significant factor influencing the viral community structure. Functionally, the IBS virome was enriched in auxiliary metabolic genes involved in carbon metabolism and neurotransmitter precursor synthesis (histidine and tryptophan metabolism), as well as a distinct profile of virulence factors and antibiotic resistance genes. Furthermore, in a specific cohort, certain viral taxa were significantly correlated with the severity of anxiety and depression. Machine learning models based on viral signatures achieved robust performance for IBS subtyping (area under the curve = 0.92). This study establishes a global baseline for the IBS gut virome, demonstrating that viral communities are dynamically shaped by geography and disease subtypes while encoding gene repertoires with the potential to influence host physiology, thereby providing a foundational resource for precision medicine.IMPORTANCEResearch on the human gut microbiome in IBS has focused primarily on bacteria, leaving the viral component as a vast and poorly understood reservoir. By profiling over 1,000 human samples globally, this study characterizes the taxonomic and functional features of the IBS gut virome. We demonstrate that these viral communities vary across geographic populations and IBS subtypes and are enriched in specific auxiliary metabolic genes, virulence factors, and antibiotic resistance genes. In addition, certain viral profiles show significant correlations with patient psychological symptoms such as anxiety and depression. This study also evaluates the potential of virome-based diagnostic biomarkers. Consequently, our findings provide a valuable reference for future in-depth research into the specific roles and mechanistic contributions of the gut virome in the pathogenesis of IBS.

title: Nitrate potentiates kanamycin activity in bacteria through metabolic reprogramming and CpxR-associated respiratory activation
abstract: Antibiotic resistance in foodborne bacteria profoundly compromises the effectiveness of antimicrobial therapies and represents a persistent global threat to public health and livestock production. There is therefore an urgent need to develop adjuvant strategies that can improve the activity of existing antibiotics against drug-resistant pathogens. In this study, comparative proteomic profiling of kanamycin-susceptible and laboratory-passaged kanamycin-resistantserovar Enteritidis (. Enteritidis) revealed coordinated differences in the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, nitrogen metabolism, and the respiratory electron transport chain. The resistant strain displayed reduced NADH production, proton motive force (PMF), and intracellular kanamycin accumulation. Because these proteomic analyses were performed under antibiotic-free conditions and whole-genome sequencing was not conducted, these differences are interpreted as physiological features associated with the resistant phenotype rather than as evidence of the specific genetic mechanism responsible for the increased kanamycin MIC. Mechanistically, nitrate acted as a potent kanamycin adjuvant by increasing cellular bioenergetic activity through the nitrate-glutamine-glutamate-associated pathway. Nitrate increased NADH production, enhanced TCA cycle activity, and elevated PMF, thereby increasing intracellular kanamycin accumulation. Nitrate also altered CpxR-associated regulation of respiratory genes, providing an additional route by which respiratory activity could be enhanced. Genetic disruption of nitrate transport or selected metabolic and regulatory components attenuated nitrate-mediated potentiation, supporting contributions from both metabolic flux and CpxR-associated respiratory regulation. Importantly, nitrate enhanced kanamycin-mediated killing not only in the laboratory-derived Kana-R strain but also in kanamycin-susceptible Kana-S, indicating a general kanamycin-potentiating effect rather than specific reversal of an acquired resistance mechanism. The nitrate-kanamycin combination also improved treatment outcomes against clinically resistantEnteritidis isolates, including increased survival in murine and chicken infection models. Collectively, these findings identify nitrate as a metabolic adjuvant that can potentiate kanamycin activity by increasing bacterial bioenergetics and drug accumulation. They further illustrate how bacterial physiological state can modulate aminoglycoside efficacy without establishing that nitrate reverses the underlying genetic mechanism of kanamycin resistance.IMPORTANCEAntibiotic efficacy is influenced not only by inherited resistance determinants but also by the physiological and metabolic state of bacterial cells. Our study shows that nitrate can potentiate kanamycin activity inserovar Enteritidis by enhancing central metabolism, respiratory activity, proton motive force, and intracellular drug accumulation. This potentiation was observed in both a kanamycin-resistant laboratory-passaged strain and a kanamycin-susceptible strain, supporting a general adjuvant effect rather than specific reversal of a defined resistance mechanism. The nitrate-kanamycin combination also improved outcomes in animal infection models using resistant strains. These findings identify inorganic nitrogen metabolism and CpxR-associated respiratory regulation as potential leverage points for developing aminoglycoside adjuvant strategies.

title: No strain, no gain: within-host bacterial microdiversity and human health
abstract: It is well established that within a bacterial species, genotypic and phenotypic variation leads to differences in virulence, antibiotic susceptibility, and metabolism. However, there is also increasing evidence that often multiple variants of the same species co-inhabit the same site in the human body, both during health and disease. This within-host microdiversity can develop over time for pathogens in chronic infections and has been observed for many members of the microbiota, for instance in the gut and on the skin. Research is just beginning to uncover how this within-host intra-species diversity develops and why it matters. Intra-species diversity is largely stable over time, with occasional selective sweeps of new genotypes, and the overall level of diversity is modulated by both microbe-microbe and microbe-host interactions. Furthermore, data indicate that within-host microdiversity can impact the stability of bacterial communities, their antimicrobial resistance, and the efficacy of probiotics and microbiota transplants. Here, we describe the evolutionary and ecological processes that promote high or low within-host microdiversity and the extent of this diversity in the human microbiota and in infections. In addition, we consider how microdiversity within individuals shapes the functional role of the human microbiota and the progression of disease. Together, within-host microdiversity is a newly developing way to think about the diversity of human-associated microbes, with implications in how we treat chronic infections and manipulate our microbiota to promote health.

title: Use of direct injection UHPLC-MS/MS for antibiotic population use assessment by wastewater analysis - application to laboratory and monitoring studies
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a global human health threat and wastewater analysis of antibiotics can help inform AMR policies. Accurate quantification of antibiotic use in urban populations is needed. This requires analytical methods capable of high sample throughput to support short-term laboratory antibiotic fate investigations where large sample numbers are generated, and sub-µg Lquantification limits for wastewater monitoring studies. Therefore, a direct injection ultra-high performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (UHPLC-MS/MS) method was developed for 11 representative antibiotics and metabolites with a 13 min run time and quantitation limits in the range of 0.0012-0.69 µg L. Avoiding solid phase extraction simplified sample preparation whilst mitigating potential contamination or analyte loss, additional solvent use and single-use plastics. High throughput application of the method was demonstrated by assessing antibiotic stability in laboratory-scale gravity sewers (= 6) with sampling intervals of 0, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, and 24 hours. Amoxicilloic acid, hydroxymetronidazole, trimethoprim and clarithromycin showed satisfactory short-term stability (4 h) for sampling influent wastewater at treatment plants for population use assessment. The sensitivity of the direct injection methodology was demonstrated by random influent wastewater monitoring (= 5) at three treatment plants in North-East Scotland during August by 24 h pseudo flow-weighted composite sampling. This revealed amoxicillin, metronidazole, trimethoprim and clarithromycin use ranged from 263 to 3559 mg/1000 people per day. This was 0.5 to 1.8 times the corresponding average daily prescribed quantity (calculated from total August prescribing) within the treatment plant's catchment area, highlighting differences in prescription and consumption levels across locations. Findings demonstrated direct injection UHPLC-MS/MS to be ideal for supporting population use assessment of antibiotics through application to laboratory and monitoring wastewater studies.

title: From Sequence to Structure: AlphaFold and the AI Revolution in Aquaculture Drug Discovery and Vaccine Design
abstract: Global aquaculture faces an escalating disease and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) crisis, exacerbated by climate-driven physiochemical shifts and intensive farming practices. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and structural biology, spearheaded by AlphaFold, represents a paradigm shift in aquatic pharmacology, transitioning the field from empirical trial-and-error to rational in silico design. This review critically evaluates the application of AI-driven tools in aquaculture drug discovery and vaccine development. We examine the evolution of AlphaFold in predicting complex host-pathogen interactions and facilitating de novo drug design. Concurrently, we highlight critical limitations stemming from the reliance on multiple sequence alignment (MSA) depth rather than mere PDB taxonomic composition, the unreliability of direct molecular docking due to apo conformations, and the dynamic nature of psychrophilic adaptations in aquatic environments. Furthermore, we assess next-generation structural vaccinology, including reverse vaccinology and pre-fusion antigen stabilization, alongside the integration of nanomaterial-based delivery systems to overcome aquatic pharmacokinetic barriers. The synergy of AI with CRISPR/Cas technologies and multimodal large language models (MM-LLMs) for disease management is also explored. Despite unprecedented computational capabilities, significant bottlenecks remain, including a severe lack of species-specific omics data, the indispensability of in vivo wet-lab validation, and lagging regulatory frameworks. Ultimately, realizing the potential of precision aquatic medicine requires developing aquaculture-specific databases, addressing the ecological risks of open-water deployment, and democratizing these technologies for small-scale farmers to ensure sustainable, equitable, and resilient global aquaculture.

title: Molecular detection of biofilm-related genes and antimicrobial resistance patterns in Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolates from Northern Iran
abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is widely recognized as one of the primary opportunistic pathogens responsible for a wide range of nosocomial infections, notably in immunocompromised patients. Antibiotic resistance and biofilm formation, as two major virulence factors of P. aeruginosa, are related to the persistence of prolonged infections. This study was designed to (1) evaluate the frequency of multidrug-resistant (MDR) P. aeruginosa in northern Iran and (2) analyze the frequency of biofilm-associated genes and their correlation with antimicrobial patterns. Clinical samples (n = 80) were collected from ICUs and other wards and processed for the isolation and identification of P. aeruginosa. Antimicrobial susceptibility was assessed using disk diffusion. PCR was performed to target the biofilm-associated genes. Out of 80 P. aeruginosa isolates, the prevalence of isolates was highest in the ICU (57.5%), and sputum was the most common specimen type (37%). Piperacillin/tazobactam demonstrated the highest activity (76.2% susceptible), followed by amikacin (52.5% susceptible). Notably, 45% of the isolates were MDR, 52.5% were XDR, while 2.5% were neither MDR nor XDR. The biofilm-associated genes ppyR and pslA were detected in 92.5% and 87.5% of the isolates, respectively, whereas pelA was found in 85% of the isolates. Among the 59 pelA, ppyR, and pslA-positive isolates, 47.45% were MDR, 42.37% were XDR, and 10.18% were non-MDR/XDR. Based on these outcomes, we strongly recommend strict infection prevention and control strategies to limit the transmission of MDR-PA, particularly in hospital settings. Piperacillin/tazobactam remains relatively effective; however, its administration should be guided by antimicrobial stewardship guidelines.

title: Reclassification of the type B CAT family and identification of the novel chloramphenicol acetyltransferase CatB14 in Riemerella anatipestifer
abstract: Chloramphenicol resistance in Riemerella anatipestifer is primarily mediated by chloramphenicol acetyltransferases (CATs). Inconsistent nomenclature of the CatB superfamily in public databases currently complicates the genomic surveillance of these resistance determinants. In this study, we tested the subtype scheme recorded in the NCBI Reference Gene Catalog against a complete pairwise amino acid identity matrix, applying a ≥ 80% identity criterion. The analysis supports the existing type B-1 to type B-5 subtypes, assigns two previously unassigned sequences to Type B-2, and recommends retirement of the polyphyletic catB12 designation. Under this framework, the catB gene previously reported in R. anatipestifer CH-2 is reclassified as Type B-6, for which we propose the designation catB13, and a novel variant forming an independent lineage (Type B-7) is identified, for which we propose the designation catB14. Functional analysis and site-directed mutagenesis of the predicted catalytic dyad (Y29/H78) confirmed that CatB14 is an active enzyme conferring chloramphenicol resistance; its activity decreased at 3 mM chloramphenicol concentrations relative to that at 2 mM, a pattern compatible with substrate inhibition. Comparative analysis of genetic contexts identified two arrangements of the catB14-floR module: one associated with mobA/mobB and ISCR2, the other chromosomal and associated with IS1182 within a multidrug-resistance region. We propose a two-configuration evolutionary model for the stabilization of the determinant, although this relationship is inferred from the comparison of genetic contexts rather than demonstrated experimentally. This work provides a standardized nomenclature framework for the CatB superfamily and describes the genetic contexts in which catB14 occurs.

title: Catheter-related bloodstream infection reduction using systematic training in a Portuguese tertiary care hospital
abstract: Catheter-related bloodstream infections (CRBSI) are a major cause of morbidity, mortality, and increased healthcare costs among hospital-acquired infections. To reduce CRBSI, the Infection Prevention and Control and Antimicrobial Resistance Program (UL-PPCIRA) reviewed current guidelines and implemented an intensive training project for healthcare professionals.
